title: How do you deploy a change to this system without risking an outage?
summary: Tests whether you can name a concrete rollout mechanism and the metric that gates each step, not just "we'd test it first."

slides.markdown:
"We test it before deploying" doesn't cover the failure modes that only show up under real production traffic — a subtle serialization bug, a resource leak, an edge case in traffic your staging environment never sees.

This question tests whether you have a concrete rollout mechanism — a canary, a gradual ramp — plus a specific metric that gates each step and a fast rollback path. "We'd test it first" is table stakes, not the answer; the answer is what happens *after* tests pass, once the change meets real users.

Ask whether this is a stateless service, a stateful one, or a schema change — each needs a genuinely different approach. A stateless service can be canaried and rolled back cleanly at any point; a stateful change or a database migration might not be reversible once applied.

Ask directly whether this deploy can be rolled back cleanly, or whether it involves an irreversible step. That answer determines whether "roll back if it breaks" is even a valid safety net, or whether you need a different strategy — like an additive, backward-compatible migration — because there's no rollback to fall back on.

Canary a small percentage of traffic, watch a specific gating metric, ramp up in stages, with a fast rollback path available at every step. A typical ramp: 1% → 10% → 50% → 100%, holding each stage until the gate metric has stayed steady for a defined window.

The two details that separate this from a vague "we'd roll it out gradually": naming the *specific* metric that gates promotion (not just "watch for problems"), and confirming rollback is fast and automatic at any stage, not a manual scramble. For how this fits a broader release process, see [rolling out a design](rolling-out-a-design).

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a canary rollout with a gate metric
slides.markdown:
![Staged rollout from 1% to 100% traffic, gated by metric checks, with automatic rollback on failure](assets/staged-rollout-gates.svg)

Each step is held until the gate metric — usually error rate and p99 latency, compared against a control group — stays steady for the hold window. Only then does traffic promote to the next stage.

If the gate metric breaches at any point, the rollback path fires automatically, not as a manual decision made under pressure.

assets.alt: Staged rollout from 1% to 100% traffic, gated by metric checks, with automatic rollback on failure

slides.markdown:
A new caching layer is deployed to 1% of traffic first. Error rate and p99 latency on that 1% are compared against a control group for 15 minutes before promoting to 10%. That 15-minute hold catches a subtle cache-serialization bug affecting 3% of requests on the canary slice — a small enough blast radius that it's caught and rolled back before it ever reaches most users.

Without the canary stage, that same bug hitting 100% of traffic at once would have meant 3% of all requests failing across the whole user base, discovered only after the fact.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: the schema-change case canarying doesn't cover
slides.markdown:
A database schema change can't just be canaried the same way application code is, because the schema is shared by every instance regardless of which code version they're running. The answer here is an **additive, backward-compatible migration**: add the new column or table without removing the old one, deploy and verify the migration itself, and only then ship the code that depends on it.

This lets old and new code run against the same schema simultaneously during the rollout window — the old code ignores the new column, the new code uses it, and neither breaks. Dropping the old column or making a destructive change only happens in a later, separate deploy once the new code is fully rolled out.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
A slow, staged canary catches more problems before they're widespread, but it delays how fast a fix or feature actually reaches every user.

| Situation | Right pace |
|---|---|
| Routine feature rollout | Full staged path — 1% → 10% → 50% → 100%, each held to its window |
| Critical hotfix for an active incident | Accept more risk, move faster — a shorter hold, or a bigger first jump |

The pace isn't fixed — it's a judgment call between the cost of a slower rollout (delayed value, delayed fix) and the cost of a faster one (more blast radius if something's wrong). Naming which situation you're in, out loud, is the actual signal here.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: the canary looked fine but the full rollout broke
slides.markdown:
The canary missed a **scale-dependent failure mode** — something the 1% traffic slice never triggered. Two common shapes: a resource leak (a connection, a memory allocation) that only matters once it accumulates under full load, since 1% traffic for 15 minutes never leaks enough to show up. Or an edge case concentrated in a traffic segment that's underrepresented in a small random canary slice — a specific client version, region, or user cohort.

The fix going forward: hold canary stages longer for anything suspected of a slow leak, and consider a canary slice deliberately weighted to include known-tricky segments rather than a pure random sample.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: the gate metric looked fine but a problem showed up an hour later
slides.markdown:
Hold each canary stage for longer than the shortest failure mode you actually care about — if a resource leak takes 45 minutes to matter, a 15-minute hold structurally can't catch it. And don't stop watching once you hit 100%: keep key metrics under closer-than-usual observation for a window even after full rollout, not just during the ramp.

This is why "the canary passed" and "the deploy is safe" aren't the same claim — the canary only proves the change survived the specific window and traffic slice you tested it against.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: deploying to 100% because "it passed staging"
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "It passed all our staging tests, so it's safe to deploy to everyone at once."

**Why it's wrong:** staging traffic, by definition, isn't real production traffic — it doesn't have production's scale, its exact traffic mix, or its edge-case-generating diversity of real users. Skipping any production-traffic verification step means the first time this change meets real conditions is at 100% exposure, with the entire user base as the test.

**Correct model:** staging tests are a necessary gate before deploying at all, never a substitute for a staged production rollout — the canary stage exists precisely because staging can't fully stand in for production.

Canary a small percentage, watch a specific gating metric (error rate, p99 latency vs. a control group), ramp up in stages, and keep a fast rollback path at every step. For schema changes, canarying alone doesn't work — use an additive, backward-compatible migration so old and new code can coexist safely.

Hold each stage longer than the slowest failure mode you're worried about, and keep watching after full rollout, not just during the ramp. "It passed staging" is a precondition for deploying, never a substitute for verifying against real production traffic.
